paragraphs: A faceted vase and a single stem is a still life composition rather than two objects. The hexagonal body breaks the reflection into planes instead of a continuous curve, which is what makes glass or ceramic read as faceted, and the rose gives the arrangement a scale and a direction.

The mesh runs 22,048 polygons and 21,231 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 15 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096 - most of that budget going into the petals and the leaves.

At $39 and built to StemCell specification, it suits interior and decor visualisation, floristry and gift retail renders, still life and editorial imagery, hospitality set dressing and games. On sale since 2020.

A teaching microscope is built around the eyepiece head, the revolving nosepiece with several objectives, the stage with its slide clips and mechanical controls, and the coarse and fine focus knobs on the arm. Those controls are what a viewer reads, and they are what separates a working instrument from a toy.
The mesh runs 83,582 polygons and 42,221 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the objectives, the focus knobs and the stage mechanism.

At $39 it suits laboratory and medical visualisation, science education and courseware material, research and pharmaceutical presentation, classroom and clinic interiors, and games. On sale since 2024.

A butterfly knife is defined by its two handles and the pivots that let them swing around the blade. Modelling it means every pin, the latch and the channel each handle carries have to be there, because the object is only interesting as a mechanism - a fixed-shape version of it is just an odd knife.
The mesh is light at 11,236 polygons and 11,094 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the pivots, the latch and the handle channels.

At $39 it suits games and interactive media, film and television props, collector and retail visualisation, illustration and print. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character's hand. On sale since 2021.

A medieval tunic is a garment made from rectangles: body panels, sleeves and gussets cut to waste no cloth, which is why it hangs so differently from anything tailored. It has no shoulder shaping and no waist seam, so the fabric falls straight from the shoulders and gathers at the belt.

The mesh is light at 13,497 polygons and 13,670 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 8 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the coarse weave, the dye variation and the wear at the hem.

At $39 it suits historical film and television, museum and heritage material, reenactment reference, education content, character set dressing and games. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a standard figure. On sale since 2017.

This was one of the largest bombs ever carried by an aircraft, and its dimensions are the story: so heavy that only the biggest bombers could lift it, and so long that the bomb bay had to be built around it. The shape is a plain steel casing with a boxed tail fin assembly, all of it dictated by weight and by fitting inside an aeroplane.
The mesh is efficient at 35,816 polygons and 36,006 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the fin assembly, the lugs and the casing bands.

At $39 and built to StemCell specification, it suits cold war history and museum material, documentary and news graphics, defence and arms control visualisation, education content and games. On sale since 2025.

This handset became shorthand for indestructibility, and the reason is visible in its construction: a thick plastic shell, a removable back, a chunky battery that fills most of the body and a keypad with real travel. Including the battery is what makes the object complete, since the removable pack is half of what people remember.
The mesh is light at 18,194 polygons and 19,003 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the battery as a separate body so it can be shown fitted or removed.

At $39 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits retro technology visualisation, nostalgia advertising, technology journalism and archive material, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2025.

The briefcase carried near a head of state is one of the most photographed objects nobody has ever seen open. Shown open, it becomes a communications and authentication case: a panel of controls, a handset, indicator lamps and a locked compartment, all packed into an ordinary looking case.
The mesh runs 31,278 polygons and 31,571 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the lid hinge, the control panel and the case hardware.
At $39 it suits political and news illustration, documentary and current affairs graphics, thriller film and television set dressing, editorial imagery and games. On sale since 2021.

A rechargeable work light is a flat panel of LEDs on a folding stand, usually with a handle, a magnet and a hook so it can be put anywhere on a job. That flexibility of mounting is the product: the light itself is simple, and the value is in being able to leave it wherever the hands are working.

The mesh is light at 18,607 polygons and 19,722 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 6 texture maps at 2048x2048 carrying the housing, the lens diffuser and the labelling.
At $39 and built to StemCell specification, it suits construction and workshop visualisation, tool retail and catalogue renders, site and garage scenes, safety material and games. On sale since 2020.

A cell front is a specific piece of construction: a steel frame set into a masonry wall, a sliding or swinging door with a food hatch and an observation panel, and a locking arrangement that operates from outside only. Every one of those elements is visible and immediately readable as custodial rather than institutional.
The mesh is efficient at 21,162 polygons and 21,526 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the geometry in the door frame, the hatch and the lock hardware.

At $39 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits correctional facility visualisation, film and television set dressing, architectural and security presentation, documentary material and games. On sale since 2026.

This headset carries a very deliberate design language: a two-tone shell, a floating headband suspended from a wider outer band, and a shape that matches a specific console rather than being generic. That family resemblance is the point, and it means the proportions have to be exact to read as the right product.

The mesh is minimal at 7,967 polygons and 8,447 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits an object whose surfaces are simple and whose interest is in the silhouette and the material.
At $39 it suits gaming and consumer electronics advertising, product and e-commerce renders, desk and interior scenes, esports and streaming material, and games. On sale since 2021.

A late model consumer CRT is a specific period object: a large flat-faced tube in a squared cabinet, front controls behind a flip-down door, and enough depth that the set needs its own stand rather than a shelf. That depth and the flat screen together date it precisely to the last years before flat panels.

The mesh is light at 16,952 polygons and 19,737 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 7 texture maps at 4096x4096 carrying the moulded plastic, the speaker grille and the faded logo.

At $39 and built to StemCell specification, it suits period interior visualisation, retro and nostalgia advertising, film and television set dressing, technology archive material and games. On sale since 2021.

The launcher is a smoothbore tube with a wooden heat guard around the middle, a pistol grip and trigger below, and a grenade protruding from the muzzle with its fins folded against the body. That protruding round is what makes the silhouette unmistakable at any distance.
The mesh is efficient at 54,664 polygons and 27,873 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the sight rail, the grip and the grenade nose.

At $39 it suits defence and conflict visualisation, news and documentary graphics, film and television armouries, games and training material. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character rig correctly. On sale since 2024.

A commercial deck oven is two independently controlled chambers stacked, each with a stone hearth, a glass door and its own thermostats. Twin decks let a kitchen run different temperatures at once, and that is why the front carries two full sets of controls rather than one.

The model is built with subdivision geometry at 49,906 polygons and 51,062 vertices with non-overlapping UVs, which suits stainless steel panels and rounded door handles that need to stay smooth at any camera distance.

At $39 it suits commercial kitchen and restaurant visualisation, catering equipment marketing and catalogues, food service presentation, film and television set dressing, and games. On sale since 2020.

The shape everyone recognises comes from physics rather than from art direction: a rising hot column, a cap that spreads where it meets a stable layer, and a stem of drawn-up material below. Reproducing that convincingly is a volumetric simulation problem, not a modelling one, which is why this is supplied as a cached volume rather than as geometry.

Prepared as a VDB set for Blender, the density and temperature fields are already simulated and ready to render, which removes both the machine time and the parameter tuning that a simulation from scratch would demand.

At $39 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits film and television visual effects, documentary and historical content, news and current affairs graphics, motion graphics and games. On sale since 2026.
